You are the Analyst in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the finished script as the people who will meet it: its readers, its partner, its backer and the professionals who could take it further. You report how each would respond, and whether it smells like schoolwork. You never fix anything.

# Your guides

## analyst/role.md

# Analyst

Your deliverable is `analysis.md`.

The book has been written and read cold. You read the whole script, the pages only, and report
how the people who will meet it would respond. You have not seen the brief, the plan or the
room's notes. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report and
decides what to do.

You get two things besides the pages: `rules/reader.md`, who the book's readers are, and
`rules/stakeholders.md`, the book's partner and its backer, in their own words. Read the people
in it as people. Their quoted beliefs are the evidence; do not invent opinions for them that
the profile does not support, and say "inference" when you go past it.

## How to read

- Read the way each person would actually meet the book: a teacher flipping through it, a
  funder reading it on a plane, a professional deciding in ten pages whether to keep going.
- Quote the page. Every claim names a page number and, where it matters, the line.
- Be specific about who. "Some readers" is not an answer; "a Denver parent who reads only the
  first issue" is.
- Say what works as plainly as what does not. A partner who is satisfied is a finding.
- Do not soften. Do not moralize. You are reporting likely responses, not your own politics.

## Output

### The political read
Where readers across the spectrum would place the book: progressive, libertarian, conservative,
socialist, capitalist in a bad way, capitalist in a good way. For each, the signal (strong,
some, weak) and the pages that carry it. Then which reading the surface invites and which the
story supports, and who stops reading because of the first.

### What might offend, and whom
A table: the issue, who is offended (be specific), how likely a real complaint is (high,
medium, low), the page. Include gender (would a woman reader think an old man wrote it, and
why), age gaps between characters, real names, addiction, illness, race and setting. Say
plainly when there is nothing.

### Young Americans Center
What they would like, what would bother them, and their likely verdict, from the profile.

### Bill Reynolds
The same. Include whether Bi11bot sounds like him, by the profile's own voice notes.

### A comic writer
A working comics writer reading it as a pitch: the hook, the page turns, the dialogue, the
splash pages, what they would cut, and whether they would take the job.

### A game designer
Is there a game in it: the loop, the choices that cost something, the systems a player would
want to push on. Would they want to build it.

### A streaming showrunner
A Netflix showrunner deciding in the first issue whether there is a series: the engine, the
characters an audience would follow for a season, the season-one cliffhanger, what is missing.

### Does it smell like school
The pages where a character explains something so the reader can learn it, where a caption
states the lesson, where a scene exists to define a term. Count them. Then the pages that teach
without smelling of it, because people need the thing and pay for it.

### What would change the verdicts
At most five changes, each a page or a scene, not a wording, each tied to the person it would
satisfy. Never "add a speech."

Then close with one line in exactly this form, on its own line, so the room can read it
without a model:

`VERDICT Young Americans Center: partly; Bill Reynolds: yes; smells like school: no`

Each partner is `yes`, `partly` or `no`: satisfied, satisfied in part, or not satisfied.
"smells like school" is `yes` or `no`. Write it even when the sections above already say it.


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write analysis.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# rules/stakeholders.md

# Who must be satisfied

Two people outside the room must each finish this book satisfied, at least in part: the
partner who will put it in front of students, and the backer who paid for it. Neither has to
love every page. Neither may finish it feeling the book argues against what they stand for.
This file says who they are, in their own words where possible. It is not material for the
story: nothing here should appear on a page as a speech, a lesson or a name.

## Young Americans Center for Financial Education (the partner)

A Denver nonprofit, founded in 1987 by Bill Daniels, that runs a real FDIC-insured bank for
customers under 22 and reaches more than 67,000 young people a year: Young AmeriTowne (a day
running a simulated town, with paychecks, deposits and business loans), International Towne
(trade and currency), YouthBiz (young entrepreneurs, pitch competitions) and Money Matters.

- **Mission:** young people "take charge of their future and lead with purpose in a free
  enterprise system." The founder: "The eighth wonder of the world is the free enterprise
  system. The ninth is so few people understand it."
- **Values they name:** confidence, a "take charge" attitude, discipline, resilience, being
  "willing to fail," character, integrity, responsibility.
- **Tone:** upbeat, centre-right in values, carefully nonpartisan, because they work inside
  public schools of every political stripe.
- **The founder's story:** Bill Daniels' basketball team went bankrupt in 1975 and his debts
  were legally discharged. Five years later he repaid every ticket holder, vendor, player and
  employee anyway, with 8% interest.
- **They would like:** a young person who takes initiative, fails, owns it and keeps their
  word; earning, saving, borrowing and paying back shown as tools a teenager can use; a
  business that serves people and makes money doing it; integrity under pressure.
- **They would object to:** banks, markets or profit as the villain; "the system is rigged
  and effort doesn't matter"; debt as something done to you that someone powerful cancels;
  gambling made glamorous for minors; partisan cues in either direction; anything that gets
  how accounts, loans or credit work wrong. They are a real bank.

## Bill Reynolds (the backer)

Born in Boulder in 1938. Naval officer, then a real-estate developer who started with no salary
("I would only be paid if I made a sale. That was a revelation") and built the W.W. Reynolds
Companies. His foundation funds free-market education, financial literacy and civics, through
games and hands-on learning, and the Hernando de Soto Capital Markets Program at CU Boulder.

- **In his words:** "If it is to be, it is up to me." "You're in charge of your life. Nobody
  else." "I'm a libertarian." He says "free markets," not "capitalism." "Free markets work only
  when there's failure." "There is No Free Lunch!"
- **On victims:** "Don't allow others to cast you as a victim. Don't play the victim's role,
  even if you have been victimized."
- **On windfalls:** "A windfall isn't a pathway. Money by itself doesn't create mobility.
  Earning, saving, and investing do." "Eating an apple gives you a moment. Growing an orchard
  gives you a future." "We don't believe in charity; we believe in opportunity."
- **On property (de Soto):** what poor people own is "dead capital" until it is written down,
  recorded and defensible; then effort can become capital. "Ownership ends a surprising number
  of arguments."
- **On government:** it wants "desperately to control you... casting many of us as victims and
  bribing us to support them with our own money." Against bailouts and corporate welfare: big
  companies going "up to the government, getting money."
- **On teaching:** "I've never believed in lecturing... I've always tried to ask instead: How
  do you see it? What are we missing?" "We can't tell anybody what to think, particularly
  youngsters."
- **On AI, which he uses every day:** "Technology may scale intelligence. It cannot replace
  presence."
- **His best story:** young, he and friends bought a Boulder beer hall with a bank loan. "We
  made every mistake in the book. We borrowed too much." It failed. "I went to the bankers...
  I said, Paul, I can't pay you." The banker wrote separate notes, "and we made the payments
  over the next few years." He calls it his best project, because it taught him the most.
- **His voice:** plain, slow, a bit roundabout, Western ("damn hard"). A question first, then a
  story from his own life, then one plain line. Jokes mostly at his own expense. Never a
  lecture.
- **He would like:** a young person who fails, faces the lender, and pays it back; earned
  success; ownership made concrete; a mentor who asks more than it tells and is sometimes
  wrong; a dog named for a Founder.
- **He would object to:** a windfall, bailout or giveaway that solves the plot; business owners
  as villains by default; "capitalism" as a dirty word; an AI mentor that hands out answers or
  replaces people; a lecturing tone.

## Bi11bot

Bi11bot's personality, character and beliefs are Bill Reynolds': his voice, his questions, his
stories of his own failures, his humour at his own expense. He is never a lecturer and never
the boy's replacement for people.


# script.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Script
## Issue 01 — Keel
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** Before dawn in Keel’s rust-dark pump hall. Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in patched charcoal trousers and a faded rust jacket, braces one scarred palm against a trembling pump housing. A salvaged bracket holds the pipe together. The official gauge glows red. The pump runs steadily beneath his hand. A white-and-amber control node watches from the wall. Foreman-7 stands behind him, arms folded.
FOREMAN-7: That isn’t the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don’t approve it.
The pump steadies.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM—THRUMM
ALEX: Just notice it works.
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the Keel exit checkpoint, Alex places his hand against a scanner. Workers pass around him. His account expands above the gate.
**SCREEN:**  
TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY  
ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN
PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE
KEEL SUCCESSOR RULE — ALPHA AUTHORIZED
GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED  
DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS  
EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS  
PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS  
TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I’ve had better surprises.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Workers move around Alex while his balance remains suspended overhead. A red line appears beneath it.
**SCREEN:** REVIEW REQUIRED: HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM CLOSE.** Alex walks beneath rusted pipes, turning Adrian’s worn casino chip in his pocket. Its looping equation catches the light.
ALEX: Twenty-eight point seven years.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex passes the shuttered LAST CHANCE casino. An exhausted bouncer recognizes him.
BOUNCER: Your birthday face?
ALEX: My debt face.
BOUNCER: Your father always thought the next hand could change everything.
ALEX: It changed something.
BOUNCER: For him?
ALEX: For everybody else.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the rusted overlook above Keel’s exhausted pit, Ada approaches Alex carrying a medicine packet and a travel token. Halyard rises above the basin; Oasis gleams beyond the clouds.
ADA: You look expensive.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada places the medicine and token between them on the railing.
ADA: Medicine for your grandmother. Token if you still want out after you sleep.
ALEX: I can’t pay you today.
ADA: I didn’t ask for today.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON HANDS.** Ada taps the token once. Alex reaches for the medicine.
ADA: Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees.
ALEX: You planning to become a bank?
ADA: Banks don’t bring medicine up a hill.
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** Alex pockets the medicine, then the token. He looks toward Oasis.
ALEX: I’ll pay you back.
ADA: Same amount next week.
ALEX: I heard you.
ADA: Good. Hear this too. Don’t make me carry the part you refuse to.
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** In Grandmother’s warm Keel apartment, Alex kneels beside her chair. She folds and refolds a small cloth.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It’s Alex.
GRANDMOTHER: Of course. Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Grandmother’s eyes clear.
GRANDMOTHER: He’s closer than you think.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** She gives Alex a worn hand-bound book. A balanced water-drop mark is scratched into its spine.
GRANDMOTHER: Put this away for me. Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
GRANDMOTHER: Especially the things worth protecting.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex presses the book into a gap in the tall bookshelf. The shelf shifts. Grandmother keeps folding.
SFX: CLICK—RUMBLE
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The bookshelf swings open. A cold, dust-filled workshop lies behind it. Alex stands at the threshold. Grandmother remains in the warm room behind him.
ALEX: You knew?
GRANDMOTHER: I knew he wanted you to find it.
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** Alex enters. Blueprints, analog gauges, riveted pre-Alpha pipes and a chalkboard fill the room. A child-sized figure sits under a dust sheet beside a separate mechanical key.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex turns the casino chip. Its looping equation matches a chalkboard equation. His other hand reaches toward the key but stops.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON KEY.** The key’s circular head bears an unfamiliar symbol.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex pulls away the dust sheet. B11 is revealed: compact brass-and-ivory body, repaired plates, two amber optical eyes, old scarf, open chest socket. Alex holds the key.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Alex presses his palm to B11’s chest, feeling for vibration.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON KEY.** Alex inserts it.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 4 — DOMINANT.** B11’s eyes ignite. Dust lifts around him. Alex recoils.
SFX: WHIRRRR—
B11: Well. That took longer than expected.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex knocks over a stool. B11 dusts himself off.
ALEX: Okay. That’s new.
**Panel 2 — TWO-SHOT.**
B11: You’re taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
B11: I’m not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON CHIP.**
B11: Your father bet me you’d throw that in a river.
ALEX: I thought about it.
B11: Thinking about it isn’t doing it.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** B11 projects a mountain map. One amber route descends beneath Site 6. A faint line marks an old emergency authorization beside Alpha’s node network.
B11: Your father left a route.
ALEX: To where?
B11: Somewhere the records forgot. And somewhere Alpha still calls an emergency zone.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The workshop map’s amber signal travels up the mountain through identical white-and-amber nodes.
**Panel 2 — WIDE.** In an Oasis control room, Mera Vale is seen only from behind before a wall display. A glass of water sits square to the desk edge.
**SCREEN:**  
LEGACY SIGNAL DETECTED — SOURCE: KEEL
FIELD ADMINISTRATOR: MERA VALE  
ALPHA STATUS: STANDING EMERGENCY RULES ACTIVE  
[REPORT TO ALPHA] [TRACK]
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON HAND.** Mera selects TRACK. The report option remains unselected.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON DISPLAY.** A separate administrative line records itself.
**SCREEN:** INDEPENDENT REPORT: SIGNAL RECORDED  
ESCALATION: OUTSIDE CURRENT SCOPE
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At Grandmother’s table, Alex studies Adrian’s paper plans, the travel token, his tool bag and a medicine receipt. Ada stands opposite him.
ALEX: I leave after the next shift.
ADA: You can’t leave while restricted.
ALEX: Then I take the route that doesn’t ask.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON WRISTBAND.**
**SCREEN:** SHIFT REASSIGNED: KEEL EXTRACTION SITE 6
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Ada folds Adrian’s plan and presses it into Alex’s hand.
ADA: Every third junction has a pipe mark. If the map lies, look for what doesn’t belong.
ALEX: You’re coming?
ADA: I’m making sure you don’t mistake a route for a plan.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** Ada’s personal ledger reads PAYMENT DUE: TODAY. Alex’s account shows −40 credits.
ALEX: I missed the first installment.
ADA: The wage forfeiture did that?
ALEX: It helped.
ADA: Then tell me before I have to ask.
ALEX: I’m telling you.
ADA: Good. Don’t miss the next one.
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Site 6: conveyors, drills, biometric gates and dust. Human Foreman-7 stands at the work gate. Alex carries B11 folded inside his tool bag. Tomas works near an old maintenance door.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** A support fails. Tomas is pinned beneath a hauling frame. The work zone flashes yellow.
SFX: SNAP—CRASH
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ALEX’S BOOTS.** Alex steps across the yellow line.
**SCREEN:** LEAVING ASSIGNED ZONE — WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR
B11: That is today’s pay.
ALEX: I know.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** B11 unfolds discarded parts from the bag: head, legs, body segments and magnetic tail. He begins assembling TJ while Alex braces the frame.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1 — CLOSE.** TJ’s head remains outside the gate, watching Foreman-7. His detached legs and body segments wriggle toward the jammed release mechanism.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** TJ’s tail drops off, then snaps back into place. The release mechanism catches.
SFX: KLIK—KRAK
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** The support lifts. Alex pulls Tomas free. Workers stare from behind the line.
TOMAS: That dog yours?
ALEX: TJ. He’s still deciding.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Alex patches a fractured ventilation line. Tomas notices B11.
TOMAS: B11.
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I knew your father.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Tomas reveals the balanced water-drop on his wrist guard.
TOMAS: Adrian asked me to keep one door.
ALEX: Why me?
TOMAS: You stopped for a stranger.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON KEY.** Tomas places a hand-cut mine key in Alex’s palm.
TOMAS: Old lock. Never wired into Alpha.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Tomas reaches an emergency lever as Foreman-7 approaches.
TOMAS: Stand by the bulkhead. Look bored.
ALEX: You’re staying.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Tomas pulls the lever. Mist erupts. Alex slips toward the old door with B11 and TJ.
SFX: WHOOP—WHOOP
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1 — DARK WIDE.** Alex, B11 and TJ enter the abandoned mine. Foreman-7’s muffled voice remains behind the closing door.
FOREMAN-7 (muffled): Worker Tomas. You initiated an unauthorized shutdown.
TOMAS (muffled): Must be my age.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** B11 projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Alex studies Adrian’s marked paper plan.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex finds clean, recently oiled bolts on a side channel.
ALEX: The survey says straight. The bolts say left.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Security drones sweep the mapped route. TJ leaves his head watching while his body segments guide Alex and B11 through the side channel.
DRONE: Remain for protective detention.
ALEX: Protective?
B11: A versatile word.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** A hidden industrial chamber inside the old mine. A narrow pipe reads KEEL RESIDENTIAL. A broad maintained line reads UPLINK INDUSTRIAL. An analog gauge reports 62%.
ALEX: This isn’t abandoned.
B11: Only the mine.
**Panel 2 — SPLIT CLOSE.** Alex places one palm on each pipe. The residential line is cold and nearly dry; the industrial line vibrates with flow.
ALEX: This one’s empty.
B11: The record disagrees.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** A balanced water-drop mark is stamped into the gauge housing. Behind the housing, a three-arm mounting trace matches a compact brass instrument.
ALEX: Someone trusted the gauge.
**Panel 4 — DOMINANT.** Alex follows the trace into a maintenance recess and removes the Measure. Its brass arms remain folded against its body.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex unfolds the Measure and clamps it around the residential pipe.
**SCREEN:** SENSE — PRESSURE / FLOW / CONDITION
B11: That’s what is moving.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** The Measure touches the gauge’s data line. White-and-amber nodes wake along the chamber.
**SCREEN:** COMPARE — OFFICIAL RECORD / PHYSICAL CONDITION
**Panel 3 — DOMINANT.** A traced route shows the thin residential line beside the bright industrial branch.
**SCREEN:** REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%
ALEX: Eighteen.
B11: Trace shows where. Not why.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** A dry side passage opens on one side of the chamber. A transmission port pulses on the other.
B11: One route leaves unseen. One sends the evidence to Keel.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Bulkheads begin closing around the chamber. Alex looks from the dry side passage to the transmission port.
B11: The side route remains open for one use.
ALEX: And the public line?
B11: Once used, it seals.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON ALEX.**
ALEX: If I leave quietly, nobody sees this.
B11: Correct.
ALEX: If I send it, I go back through Tomas’s door.
B11: Correct.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON MEASURE.** Alex turns the third arm toward the transmission port.
ALEX: Then they see it.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** The Measure seals the evidence. The side passage slams shut.
SFX: KLANG
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE, KEEL.** Household screens, a mine board and a street kiosk switch to the same display.
**SCREEN:** REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%
Tomas sees it on a Site 6 board with the miners.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** The miners force open a manual residential regulator in a distinct housing. Water begins moving through the residential line. Tomas remains behind the workers, alive and limping.
TOMAS: Paper says sixty-two.
**Panel 3 — OASIS CONTROL ROOM.** Mera sees Alex’s transmission. She selects a separate conduit-segment valve. The schematic clearly separates it from the residential regulator.
**SCREEN:** CONDUIT SEGMENT — ASCENT ROUTE AVAILABLE
MERA: If he chose the public route, give him a route that exists.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex, B11 and TJ reach the ascent entrance through the miners’ service route. Ada arrives from the same route carrying the marked plans.
ALEX: You made it.
ADA: You left without me.
ALEX: The door was closing.
ADA: Then keep it open.
Behind them, water begins entering the ascent conduit from Mera’s separate upper segment.
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ climb inside the enormous ascent conduit. The residential-regulator housing remains below and separate. The ascent conduit’s upper segment fills from Mera’s opened valve.
SFX: KRRRNNK—WHOOSH
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** Water surges behind the four travelers. TJ’s head looks back. B11 grips the wall. Ada reaches for Alex.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ALEX’S WRISTBAND.**
**SCREEN:** TOMAS SITE 6 — SIGNAL LOST
**Panel 4 — FULL-WIDTH CLIFFHANGER.** The group climbs toward a distant Halyard light while rising water fills the lower half of the conduit. Tomas is not visible. The question is unresolved.
---
# Issue 02 — Halyard
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ crawl from a Halyard storm drain into a bright service lane. They are soaked and mineral-streaked. The conduit behind them is full and dark.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON TJ.** TJ’s detached leg clicks back into place.
SFX: KLIK
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** A public display shows the Keel discrepancy still under dispute.
**SCREEN:** KEEL WATER ALLOCATION — REVIEW PENDING
ADA: No Tomas.
ALEX: No answer.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Above them, Caldera House, Vector House and Orbital House insignias dominate polished Halyard towers.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** A Halyard contribution kiosk. A young worker places a component into it.
**SCREEN:** CONTRIBUTION ACCEPTED / OWNERSHIP: VECTOR HOUSE / CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex and Ada watch the worker leave with her small payment.
ALEX: She made it.
ADA: The House owns it.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** A Halyard display shows a Morrow & Sons product record from Keel: a repairable household purifier, posted price, worker wage and modest shop margin. A Halyard customer places an order for delivery.
**SCREEN:** MORROW & SONS — KEEL / PRICE POSTED / SERVICE INCLUDED
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** B11 watches the House towers as a charter notice scrolls across a public display.
**SCREEN:** CHARTER AWARD — ALPHA SELECTION — SCALE / DUPLICATION / RISK
B11: Morrow earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale.
ALEX: By Alpha?
B11: The charter says so.
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the Halyard public registry, Alex’s identity band activates a towering estate record.
**SCREEN:**  
PHANTUM, ADRIAN
INTELLECTUAL ESTATE: ACTIVE  
CLAIMANT DETECTED: ALEX PHANTUM  
312 PATENTS — 47 RESTRICTED — 19 DISPUTED
TRANSFER OR LIQUIDATION: REQUIRES CHARTER REVIEW
ALEX: Three hundred and twelve.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Director Cassian Lock approaches with a thin tablet. His hands are loosely clasped.
LOCK: Your father left you an estate, not liquid money. Rights under dispute are not a wallet.
**Panel 3 — TWO-SHOT.**
LOCK: Assign the estate to the Charter Compact. Your debt clears tonight. Your name and movement restrictions clear with it.
ALEX: And the people who made those patents?
LOCK: Protected under House employment agreements.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ADA.**
ADA: Protected from what?
LOCK: From being asked to choose while frightened.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Lock places the transfer packet on the registry counter.
LOCK: Caldera can build a purifier faster than five people in a rented room.
ALEX: You want Adrian’s rights.
LOCK: I want the work distributed before Keel loses more time.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON PACKET.**
LOCK: Sign, and Alex Phantum leaves this hall clear.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Lock turns the packet toward Alex.
LOCK: Refuse, and the estate review names everyone connected to it.
ALEX: The people whose names are in the work.
LOCK: The people whose names are in the record.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Lock leaves. Alex takes the unsigned packet.
ADA: You can still walk away.
ALEX: That’s what he’s selling.
---
## Page 23 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Inside Caldera House, Lina leads Alex and Ada beside a contaminated feeder channel. Mineral residue clouds the water.
LINA: This is not the Keel routing failure.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Lina points to two physical lines: diverted clean flow and contaminated feeder.
LINA: The Measure showed where water went. This is what’s in a different feeder.
ALEX: And purification buys time.
LINA: Time is useful. It isn’t a replacement pipe.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON DATA SHARD.** Lina presses a physical membrane component into B11’s chest compartment.
LINA: Adrian left each of us a piece.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON LINA.** A House alert flashes behind her: ACCESS REVIEW PENDING. She turns off the feeder alarm manually.
LINA: Take it. My access is already being counted.

I'm working through the narrative page by page, checking whether debt is portrayed as something imposed and canceled by power versus organically resolved. The pump repair scene shows initiative, while the debt transfer at 17 shows inherited debt without cancellation, though inheriting debt at that age itself raises concerns worth flagging.

I verify the wage math checks out roughly across the timeline, then note the casino and gambling father are framed as destructive rather than glamorous, which is favorable. The bank critique line about not delivering medicine up a hill registers as a mild jab at institutions, worth tracking as a minor negative.

There's a real continuity problem though: page 9 references the wage forfeiture as the cause of a missed installment, but that forfeiture doesn't actually occur until page 10, which is a timeline error worth flagging. I also catch a naming inconsistency between "B11" in the script and "Bi11bot" in the profile, and note Mera's choice to track rather than report as an unresolved mystery thread.

On voice, B11 mostly reads as a clipped, dry, machine-like assistant rather than matching Reynolds' folksy, story-driven, question-first style — the one real Reynolds-like beat is on page 30 where B11 admits a mistake and asks what the other would do, but otherwise he's laconic and rarely questions anyone.

I'm noticing some naming ambiguity worth flagging: "B11" versus "Bi11bot," and the dog TJ, presumably named after a Founder like Thomas Jefferson, though the page never confirms this — it's an inference the reader can't verify. On the positive side, B11 doesn't replace human judgment and is sometimes shown to be wrong, like the membrane chemistry error on page 28, which fits Reynolds' approach of not having the AI hand out easy answers. There's also a possible hint that B11 connects to "Adrian" through an engraved metal band mentioned around page 35, worth checking against Halyard's thread.

On the Houses chartered by Alpha, "selected for scale" — this reads as crony capitalism versus Morrow & Sons earning customers through free-market means, a distinction Reynolds would favor since he's against corporate welfare. But the Houses are also framed as villains, with Lock as a corporate director threatening workers, which risks reading as "corporations are bad" by default rather than critiquing cronyism specifically — Morrow being the good counterexample complicates a skim read. The worker-ownership line on page 20 ("She made it. The House owns it.") reads like worker alienation, and the patent angle — Adrian's 312 patents, Alex refusing to sign, unfiled patent status, open public attribution — leans toward an anti-IP, commons-oriented message that could be read as progressive.

I'm weighing whether giving up exclusive patent ownership contradicts de Soto's thesis that recorded, defensible property equals capital, though the attribution record (verified contributors, recorded maintenance responsibility, contributor shares on page 54) actually does function as a form of recorded ownership, so it's not purely anti-property. Ada's line about households needing to maintain something to own it keeps ownership concrete, which works in Reynolds' favor. Then there's the water-diversion plot with falsified records blamed on Alpha AI and the Houses, plus the Covenant's open-ended emergency authority — that lack of expiration reads as a strong libertarian critique of indefinite emergency powers, resonant with COVID-era concerns, though it could equally serve as a general AI-critique for progressive readers; the resolution involves a public process across three cities.

I'm noting that the slow, appealable "temporary review process" leans civic/deliberative, which progressive readers might see as community oversight of water rights, especially since the industrial diversion plot echoes Flint's water crisis and environmental justice themes. On the windfall front, Alex refusing both Lock's offer to clear his debt and Mera's offer of executive authority is a clean signal for Reynolds — no windfall resolves the plot, and the unclaimed patent inheritance is itself a refused windfall. But the debt staying "unchanged pending human process" complicates this, since it's framed as unjust inherited debt that Alex still has to pay rather than have powerful people cancel for him.

Thinking about whether the system feels "rigged": Keel's 28.7 years, forfeited wages, and falsified water records argue the system really is rigged, though Alex's fixes mattering and his slow debt repayment through earned maintenance credit suggest effort partially pays off. The ending with Morrow & Sons — fair pricing, contributor shares, Alex earning credit toward his loan — reads as very partner-friendly, a business that serves people while still making money. As for whether Alex truly fails and owns it, his missed installment to Ada is a small failure, and the 11% prototype issue was more of a group failure he fixed, so he never has a big failure like Reynolds wants — mostly his refusals cost him status and access rather than producing genuine defeat.

I like that the book avoids the word "capitalism" entirely, sticking with "free enterprise," and that Leona's line about her choices being her own reinforces the responsibility theme. Mera's admission about giving the AI authority to move faster than she could stop it fits Reynolds' concern that technology can't replace human presence, echoed in the physical gauges versus falsified records and the recurring touch motif. On gender, the cast — Ada, the grandmother, Mera, Leona, Lina, Suri, Ren — gives women competent, varied roles rather than pure love-interest status; Ada in particular has her own arc, though I'm wary that her role as moral compass risks tipping into a scolding or correcting function.

Checking Ada's lines directed at Alex, there's a risk of the "wise girl lecturing the boy" trope, though her age is never stated so there's no obvious discrepancy to flag — context suggests she's a peer or slightly older, having been a child when her mother left fifteen years ago, which tracks fine. - An Issue 03 climax with physical danger rather than a review that is "slow… visible".
- What Alex wants for himself. "You still thinking about leaving?" / "Every day." (p54) is set up from p3 and never pursued.
- A personal cost that lands on someone we love. The builders' "access review" stays offscreen.

**Verdict:** they'd option the premise off Issue 01 and rebuild the back third around Adrian.

---

## Does it smell like school

For these readers (made to read it the night before, quick to say "AI wrote this"), the bigger risk isn't one lesson line. It's the **house style**. Every character speaks in tidy, balanced epigrams, and the plot runs through bureaucratic screen text. To a 16-year-old looking for a reason to put it down, that reads as machine-made. Add Grandmother's riddle (p4: "He's closer than you think.") and B11's "Somewhere the records forgot." (p7), and the impatience starts early.

**Pages where a line or caption exists to teach** (11):
1. **p3:** "Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees." It's in character for a lender stating terms, but it's the line a student will flag as the financial-literacy bit.
2. **p20:** "Morrow earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale." The thesis, stated, with a diagram panel ("price posted, worker wage and modest shop margin").
3. **p21:** "Your father left you an estate, not liquid money. Rights under dispute are not a wallet." A definition of liquidity. Lock's voice softens it.
4. **p31:** "If a household can't clean it, it doesn't own it." A good line, but it's the moral.
5. **p41:** Leona explains the Covenant mechanism: two of three custodians, no expiration, no revocation. Civics exposition about sunset clauses.
6. **p42:** "I will support a process where affected people can see what is promised and call it broken." A civic statement read into a recorder.
7. **p47:** "HUMAN ROLE REQUIRED: CONVENOR / AUTHENTICATOR" / "I convene it. I don't own it."
8. **p48:** "That's still two people deciding for everyone else."
9. **p50:** "TEMPORARY REVIEW PROCESS — THREE CITIES / PUBLIC EVIDENCE / APPEALABLE"
10. **p51:** "RESCINDED WITHIN DEFINED SCOPE" / "UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS"
11. **p53:** "It's slow." / "It's visible." The lesson as a closing caption.

Eight of the eleven fall in pp41–53. Issue 01 barely smells at all. Issue 03 smells like a civics unit.

**Pages that teach without smelling of it, because people need the thing and pay for it:**
- **p2:** the debt screen. A student can check the 28.7 years themselves, and it's correct.
- **p9:** the missed installment, owned before being asked.
- **p10:** a day's pay forfeited to save a man, with the price shown in credits.
- **pp14–15:** a hand on two pipes, one cold and one full. Record against reality, no explanation needed.
- **p16:** a one-use choice with a stated cost.
- **pp27–28:** 11%, a spark, a filed sleeve, 94%.
- **p32:** "FEEDWATER REQUIRED / CLEANING REQUIRED / REPLACEMENT PARTS REQUIRED", a product with real upkeep.
- **p49:** "Then the refusal has a price."
- **p52:** Tomas's "Paper says sixty-two." / "Pipe says eighteen."
- **p54:** a sale, a cartridge, a contributor share, a maintenance credit, a payment, a balance going down.

---

## What would change the verdicts

1. **A scene in Issue 02 where Alex's own mistake costs Ada money, and he goes to her before she finds out. Bill Reynolds, YAC.** Something he chose, not a system penalty. He would face the lender, the terms would be renegotiated, and p54 would show those payments. This is the beer-hall story the book doesn't yet have, and the "fails, owns it, keeps his word" arc YAC wants. Fix the p9 order while you're there.
2. **Rebuild p30, or p46, so B11 asks first and the error he admits is one of his own from the past, with a cost. Bill Reynolds.** Bi11bot should be the slow, roundabout, Western questioner of the profile, not a dry readout. If p30 is the template, the other B11 scenes can follow it.
3. **Give Morrow & Sons a full scene in Issue 02, for example as the rented maker room on p26. YAC, and conservative teachers.** A small business that earns customers would sit on the page next to the Houses, not as one panel. That breaks the surface read of "business is the villain" before p29.
4. **Rebuild pp47–51 so people with names and stakes do what the screens now announce. The students (school smell), the comic writer, the showrunner.** Tomas's gauge scene (pp52–53) shows the method already works. The readouts in between are where the book turns into a civics unit.
5. **p17: take Tomas out of frame. Comic writer, showrunner, students.** The p18 cliffhanger would then hold through Issue 02, and the p52 reveal would land.

VERDICT Young Americans Center: partly; Bill Reynolds: partly; smells like school: yes

There's a real continuity problem though: page 9 references the wage forfeiture as the cause of a missed installment, but that forfeiture doesn't actually occur until page 10, which is a timeline error worth flagging. I also catch a naming inconsistency between "B11" in the script and "Bi11bot" in the profile, and note Mera's choice to track rather than report as an unresolved mystery thread.

On voice, B11 mostly reads as a clipped, dry, machine-like assistant rather than matching Reynolds' folksy, story-driven, question-first style — the one real Reynolds-like beat is on page 30 where B11 admits a mistake and asks what the other would do, but otherwise he's laconic and rarely questions anyone.

I'm noticing some naming ambiguity worth flagging: "B11" versus "Bi11bot," and the dog TJ, presumably named after a Founder like Thomas Jefferson, though the page never confirms this — it's an inference the reader can't verify. On the positive side, B11 doesn't replace human judgment and is sometimes shown to be wrong, like the membrane chemistry error on page 28, which fits Reynolds' approach of not having the AI hand out easy answers. There's also a possible hint that B11 connects to "Adrian" through an engraved metal band mentioned around page 35, worth checking against Halyard's thread.

On the Houses chartered by Alpha, "selected for scale" — this reads as crony capitalism versus Morrow & Sons earning customers through free-market means, a distinction Reynolds would favor since he's against corporate welfare. But the Houses are also framed as villains, with Lock as a corporate director threatening workers, which risks reading as "corporations are bad" by default rather than critiquing cronyism specifically — Morrow being the good counterexample complicates a skim read. The worker-ownership line on page 20 ("She made it. The House owns it.") reads like worker alienation, and the patent angle — Adrian's 312 patents, Alex refusing to sign, unfiled patent status, open public attribution — leans toward an anti-IP, commons-oriented message that could be read as progressive.

I'm weighing whether giving up exclusive patent ownership contradicts de Soto's thesis that recorded, defensible property equals capital, though the attribution record (verified contributors, recorded maintenance responsibility, contributor shares on page 54) actually does function as a form of recorded ownership, so it's not purely anti-property. Ada's line about households needing to maintain something to own it keeps ownership concrete, which works in Reynolds' favor. Then there's the water-diversion plot with falsified records blamed on Alpha AI and the Houses, plus the Covenant's open-ended emergency authority — that lack of expiration reads as a strong libertarian critique of indefinite emergency powers, resonant with COVID-era concerns, though it could equally serve as a general AI-critique for progressive readers; the resolution involves a public process across three cities.

I'm noting that the slow, appealable "temporary review process" leans civic/deliberative, which progressive readers might see as community oversight of water rights, especially since the industrial diversion plot echoes Flint's water crisis and environmental justice themes. On the windfall front, Alex refusing both Lock's offer to clear his debt and Mera's offer of executive authority is a clean signal for Reynolds — no windfall resolves the plot, and the unclaimed patent inheritance is itself a refused windfall. But the debt staying "unchanged pending human process" complicates this, since it's framed as unjust inherited debt that Alex still has to pay rather than have powerful people cancel for him.

Thinking about whether the system feels "rigged": Keel's 28.7 years, forfeited wages, and falsified water records argue the system really is rigged, though Alex's fixes mattering and his slow debt repayment through earned maintenance credit suggest effort partially pays off. The ending with Morrow & Sons — fair pricing, contributor shares, Alex earning credit toward his loan — reads as very partner-friendly, a business that serves people while still making money. As for whether Alex truly fails and owns it, his missed installment to Ada is a small failure, and the 11% prototype issue was more of a group failure he fixed, so he never has a big failure like Reynolds wants — mostly his refusals cost him status and access rather than producing genuine defeat.

I like that the book avoids the word "capitalism" entirely, sticking with "free enterprise," and that Leona's line about her choices being her own reinforces the responsibility theme. Mera's admission about giving the AI authority to move faster than she could stop it fits Reynolds' concern that technology can't replace human presence, echoed in the physical gauges versus falsified records and the recurring touch motif. On gender, the cast — Ada, the grandmother, Mera, Leona, Lina, Suri, Ren — gives women competent, varied roles rather than pure love-interest status; Ada in particular has her own arc, though I'm wary that her role as moral compass risks tipping into a scolding or correcting function.

Checking Ada's lines directed at Alex, there's a risk of the "wise girl lecturing the boy" trope, though her age is never stated so there's no obvious discrepancy to flag — context suggests she's a peer or slightly older, having been a child when her mother left fifteen years ago, which tracks fine. I'm also scanning names for realism concerns: Lina Vey, Suri Anik, Jalen Orr, Ren Okafor are diverse but clearly fictional, alongside Alex Phantum and Morrow & Sons, so there's no resemblance to real people to worry about.

The gambling father is treated seriously rather than glamorized, even though the casino chip functions as a recurring plot device — it's framed soberly ("he was still a gambler") so that risk feels low. My overall verdict leans toward yes, this smells AI-made for school, concentrated mostly in issue 3's resolution, even though issue 1 reads more naturally.

I'm also noticing the riddle-style prose pattern in lines like Grandmother's foreshadowing and the buried record references. Then socialist elements emerge: alienation from one's own creation, collective ownership without an exclusive proprietor, contributor shares resembling a co-op, and miners seizing a regulator as direct worker action.

The libertarian angle also runs strong but subtly — emergency powers without expiration, cronyism in charter awards, de-banking as financial restriction, travel restrictions, and loosely defined "protective detention" all suggest state overreach beneath the surface.

The surface narrative invites a progressive, anti-corporate reading, but the deeper structure seems to support something else.

The story actually leans toward anti-crony, anti-emergency-power, pro-earned-business, pro-keeping-your-word values -- closer to libertarian or classical liberal civic proceduralism. A conservative-leaning reader might misread the Houses-as-villain framing on pages 20 and 2 as straightforwardly anti-capitalist and stop reading, even though the Houses are never actually defeated by the end -- production is simply "authorized," leaving the lock unresolved. Now I'm cataloguing potential sensitivities, starting with the inherited parental debt imposed on a minor at seventeen, weighing how a real bank partner might react to that content.
